name: Vesugen

lead: Vesugen is a short peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) from Vladimir Khavinson's bioregulator program, described as a vascular-support peptide. People take it hoping that healthier circulation shows up as fresher, younger-looking skin.

The chain runs from vessel health to circulation to skin tone. Published work is mostly in cell cultures, where it was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged vascular cells and to limit lipid peroxidation of lipoproteins. One small Russian human report exists; skin or appearance has not been measured.

paras: Users treat it as part of a broader anti-aging peptide routine, often alongside other Khavinson bioregulators, taken in periodic courses rather than continuously. Users generally report looking for gradual, general changes over weeks to months rather than a specific visible result.
There is no systematic human safety data. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide, so product quality varies and legal status depends on the country.

angle.text: Longevity users take Vesugen as a vascular peptide, hoping better blood vessel health translates into fresher, younger-looking skin. Cell-culture studies report effects on aged vascular cells; the skin-appearance link is a theory users draw.

lead: Vesugen is a synthetic tripeptide, Lys-Glu-Asp (KED, also called T-38), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group and described as a vasoprotective peptide based on sequences from vascular-tissue extracts [1].

Published work is mostly in vitro: it was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged endothelial and tissue cultures [2][2] and to restrict lipid peroxidation of human lipoproteins [3]. A Russian-language report examined synthetic peptides in elderly patients with brain syndrome [4]. It is not an approved drug and no appearance use is documented.
infobox: Russian patent RU 2295970 (2007) on capillary resistance [1]

paras: In aged tissue-specific and endothelial cell cultures, vesugen was reported to raise Ki-67 expression, with docking analysis suggesting interaction with the MKI67 promoter [2]. It was also reported to promote differentiation in aging cell cultures [5]. In vitro, vesugen and other short peptides lacked direct antioxidant activity but modified lipoprotein structure to limit lipid peroxidation and raised red-blood-cell membrane stability [3]. Another report describes short peptides' antihypoxic properties [6].

An AI-generated encyclopedia summary attributes vesugen to Khavinson's St. Petersburg institute in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and cites a 2007 Russian patent covering a peptide substance that increases capillary resistance [1].

No studies found specific to vesugen in controlled human trials. A Russian-language report on synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome exists [4], but the sources reviewed do not allow attributing results to vesugen specifically.
